video_title: Real Conversations | Beyond the Index w/ Liz Ann Sonders
gist: Keith McCullough and Schwab's Liz Ann Sonders debate whether 2026 is a cycle top: both see rotation away from AI leaders (Nasdaq average member down 50%, Anthropic valuation falling) toward adopters like healthcare and equal-weight, with Sonders flagging an under-discussed wealth-effect risk to consumption and McCullough betting on halving inflation, Fed cuts and long Treasuries.

insights.claim: Liz Ann Sonders argues rotation has become the dominant momentum trade: periodic compression in mega-cap tech/AI leaders is offset by strength elsewhere, mirroring rolling sector recessions and expansions in the economy (e.g. a software recession alongside a semi boom).
insights.speaker: Liz Ann Sonders (guest, Schwab)
insights.so_what: Expect leadership to keep rotating; diversification can be found inside the S&P rather than requiring an exit from equities.
insights.quote: I've been saying for much of the past year that I thought rotation was the new momentum trait

insights.claim: Equal-weight S&P (RSP) has been outperforming cap-weight for more than a year, as have small caps, so the broadening trade is not a new phenomenon.
insights.speaker: Liz Ann Sonders (guest, Schwab)
insights.so_what: Equal-weight and small-cap tilts are an established, not nascent, trend; Hedgeye is long RSP.

insights.claim: The Nasdaq's maximum index-level drawdown this year is 13%, but the average member's maximum drawdown is 50% (28% for the S&P 500), showing a stealth bear market absorbed through rotation and churn.
insights.speaker: Liz Ann Sonders (guest, Schwab)
insights.so_what: Index-level calm masks severe single-stock damage; monitor breadth and member drawdowns, not just the headline index.
insights.quote: the average member maximum draw down in the NASDAQ is 50%

insights.claim: With the S&P only about 6% off its all-time high while Nvidia (roughly 9% index weight) is down 30%, other parts of the index must be offsetting the AI leaders' declines.
insights.speaker: Keith McCullough (host)
insights.so_what: Confirms broadening under the surface; the offsetting sectors (healthcare, REITs) are where Hedgeye is long.

insights.claim: Since the October 2022 bull-market low, only tech and communication services outperformed the S&P over four years while the other nine sectors underperformed, pointing to overcrowded trades that may not have fully unwound.
insights.speaker: Liz Ann Sonders (guest, Schwab)
insights.so_what: Room remains for mean-reversion into the nine laggard sectors as crowded tech positioning unwinds.

insights.claim: Keith McCullough's core longs since the October Nasdaq peak include equal-weight S&P (RSP), healthcare (his largest sector allocation) and REITs, which he says just started to break out.
insights.speaker: Keith McCullough (host)
insights.so_what: A concrete late-cycle long book: defensive/adopter sectors and equal weight against short tech-bubble exposure.

insights.claim: Sonders frames AI in three phases — create, catalyze (infrastructure buildout, possibly stunted recently) and cascade (broad diffusion through enterprises) — with performance power now shifting from AI spenders and suppliers to AI adopters.
insights.speaker: Liz Ann Sonders (guest, Schwab)
insights.so_what: The next shiny object is companies that use AI to raise efficiency, not those selling picks and shovels.
insights.quote: the shiny new object to some degree is who are the adopters and who's taking advantage of this

insights.claim: Healthcare is the low-hanging fruit of AI adoption given its inefficiency and AI advances in diagnostics, testing and disease work, which helps explain healthcare's leadership.
insights.speaker: Liz Ann Sonders (guest, Schwab)
insights.so_what: Healthcare is a prime beneficiary of the AI cascade phase and a candidate overweight.

insights.claim: The forward growth rate of the Mag 7 is now lower than that of the other 493 S&P 500 companies.
insights.speaker: Liz Ann Sonders (guest, Schwab)
insights.so_what: Erodes the growth premium justifying mega-cap concentration; supports equal-weight/broadening.

insights.claim: McCullough expects real disinflation in AI token prices, which he sees benefiting enterprises across sectors while hurting those monetizing the buildout; Sonders agrees adopters gain.
insights.speaker: Keith McCullough (host)
insights.so_what: Falling AI input costs transfer margin from AI vendors to users; favors adopters over infrastructure names.

insights.claim: Hedgeye says it is having its best year ever by using AI tools it does not pay incrementally for, an example of AI value accruing to adopters; Sonders likens it to the democratization seen with past innovations, where many late-1990s bubble winners no longer exist.
insights.speaker: Keith McCullough (host)
insights.so_what: Expect AI economic surplus to spread to users while many current 'winners' may not survive, as in the dot-com era.

themes.theme: AI bubble unwind and short book

insights.claim: McCullough is short QQQ, Nvidia, CoreWeave and the neoclouds, noting neoclouds are down 75-80%, Oracle down 60%+ and Nvidia down 30%, which he calls phase one of an actual crash.
insights.speaker: Keith McCullough (host)
insights.so_what: Positions against consensus faith in hyperscalers and buildout beneficiaries.

insights.claim: Anthropic's valuation peaked around $2 trillion while revenue growth was accelerating through roughly October, and has fallen to about $1.4 trillion as filings show November revenues slowing sequentially; McCullough argues decelerating revenue and earnings growth is what compresses multiples.
insights.speaker: Keith McCullough (host)
insights.so_what: Rate-of-change deceleration, not absolute levels, drives multiple compression in AI names.
insights.quote: rate of change accelerations in topline revenue growth and earnings growth are what drive multiples

insights.claim: Hedgeye's AI bubble tracker shows 34 of 36 names in bearish trends, in drawdown, breaking down or crashing.
insights.speaker: Keith McCullough (host)
insights.so_what: Breadth of the AI breakdown is near-total; treat rallies in the cohort skeptically.

insights.claim: The Goldman most-retail-owned basket went from up 22% in May to down 15%, and it is highly correlated with fundamental long/short hedge fund performance, which has had a terrible year.
insights.speaker: Keith McCullough (host)
insights.so_what: Retail and hedge fund crowding in the same names amplifies drawdowns.

insights.claim: SOXL (3x semis) traded almost half a billion shares in one day and, even after a 22% one-day rally, remains down 81% from June, needing roughly 425% to break even; triple-levered ETFs and Nvidia are the most actively traded securities.
insights.speaker: Keith McCullough (host)
insights.so_what: Leveraged-retail wipeouts are a wealth-effect drag and a sign of speculative excess unwinding.

insights.claim: McCullough argues the Goldman Sachs CEO's upbeat CNBC comments on AI credit were self-interested, since Wall Street, VCs and Silicon Valley need Anthropic's IPO as exit liquidity.
insights.speaker: Keith McCullough (host)
insights.so_what: Discount sell-side optimism on AI ahead of a major liquidity event; IPO outcome is a key sentiment test.

insights.claim: McCullough identifies 1999-2000, 2007 and 2026 as the three economic and market-cycle tops of his career, noting the 10-year yield peaked at 5.31% this year as it did at the 2007 top; Sonders agrees on 2007 but calls 2026 'TBD'.
insights.speaker: Keith McCullough (host)
insights.so_what: Frames 2026 as a cycle peak with bond yields peaking alongside stocks, a setup for long-duration bonds.

insights.claim: S&P 500 earnings likely peaked in Q2, boosted by non-repeatable items: a 38-year high in non-operating investment gains and a fast tariff refund process.
insights.speaker: Liz Ann Sonders (guest, Schwab)
insights.so_what: Earnings comparisons get harder from here; base effects work against EPS growth.

insights.claim: Q3 reporting season shows the beat rate down to 80% and the magnitude of beats only a couple of percent, well below the four-to-six-quarter average.
insights.speaker: Liz Ann Sonders (guest, Schwab)
insights.so_what: Deteriorating earnings surprises confirm the post-peak profit slowdown.

insights.claim: McCullough calls 4% headline GDP, 4% inflation, big nominal and profit growth, and full employment 'the mother of all peaks,' and expects GDP to be cut roughly in half sequentially through H1 next year.
insights.speaker: Keith McCullough (host)
insights.so_what: Rate-of-change slowdown in growth argues for long Treasuries and against cyclical/AI equities.
insights.quote: To me, that's like the mother of all peaks.

insights.claim: McCullough forecasts inflation falling from a 3.9% peak to 1.7% by Q2 next year, aided by lower oil base effects, and expects consensus and the Fed to be surprised to the downside.
insights.speaker: Keith McCullough (host)
insights.so_what: A sharp disinflation would open the door to rate cuts and a bond rally.

insights.claim: Sonders is less confident in an inflation crash given the breadth of inflation and lagged effects such as diesel prices filtering through broader measures.
insights.speaker: Liz Ann Sonders (guest, Schwab)
insights.so_what: A key disagreement: sticky inflation would limit Fed easing and the bond-rally thesis.

insights.claim: Weak GDP despite double-digit AI capex growth is explained by imports: the latest GDP report showed a 3.3 percentage point drag from net exports because most AI buildout equipment is imported; a waning capex cycle could therefore improve the trade line.
insights.speaker: Liz Ann Sonders (guest, Schwab)
insights.so_what: AI capex is less of a domestic growth driver than assumed, and a capex slowdown may be partly cushioned in GDP.
insights.quote: the AI spend is not acrewing to the benefit of domestic growth

insights.claim: McCullough says Hedgeye is not forecasting a recession but a crash in one market component plus a slowdown, and argues falling inflation hurts corporate profits of companies that were 'gouging' consumers.
insights.speaker: Keith McCullough (host)
insights.so_what: Distinguishes a sector crash from recession; margin compression is the corporate-profit risk of disinflation.

insights.claim: Sonders sees the closest late-1990s parallel not in tech fundamentals but in the 2001 recession, when a stock-market bubble burst pulled the economy down because household equity exposure was at records — a level exceeded today.
insights.speaker: Liz Ann Sonders (guest, Schwab)
insights.so_what: A bear market in widely owned favorites could hit consumption through the wealth effect even without a financial crisis.
insights.quote: I think the wealth effect ramifications for the economy are being underd discussed

insights.claim: Unlike the dot-com bubble, where little telecom capacity was used and appreciation was all multiple, today's AI cycle has real earnings, making it not an apples-to-apples comparison.
insights.speaker: Liz Ann Sonders (guest, Schwab)
insights.so_what: Valuation risk differs from 2000, but the wealth-effect transmission channel is similar.

insights.claim: With the savings rate drawn down and K-shaped spending concentrated among upper-income households, Sonders says consumption holds if the labor market holds, but losing the labor market amid a bear market in favorites would hit consumption quickly.
insights.speaker: Liz Ann Sonders (guest, Schwab)
insights.so_what: Watch payrolls as the trigger converting a market drawdown into an economic slowdown.

insights.claim: Job-growth weakness has been concentrated in tech, as AI spenders were rewarded for restraining labor costs, while the latest strong payroll report was led by business and professional services and leisure/hospitality fell to the bottom — another rolling rotation.
insights.speaker: Liz Ann Sonders (guest, Schwab)
insights.so_what: Sector-level labor rotation mirrors market rotation; track composition, not just headline payrolls.

insights.claim: Fed pricing shows roughly a 25 bp December hike largely priced in (the 2-year jumped from 4.50% to 4.70% after CPI), with about 15% odds of 50 bp after Waller's comments; Sonders thinks a 50 bp hike would not be taken kindly by markets.
insights.speaker: Liz Ann Sonders (guest, Schwab)
insights.so_what: A 50 bp surprise is the near-term tail risk; 25 bp is consensus.

insights.claim: Ten-year BBB spreads are at roughly cycle highs, and McCullough notes spreads historically keep widening when profits slow, especially if the Fed hikes into the slowdown; Sonders expects weakness to spread from CoreWeave and suppliers to perceived safe areas.
insights.speaker: Keith McCullough (host)
insights.so_what: Expect credit contagion beyond AI names into cyclicals; reduce credit risk.

insights.claim: McCullough sees meaningful odds the Fed pivots from hiking to three-to-six cuts next year if the Nasdaq falls 25-30%, credit widens and inflation drops below 2%; Sonders thinks the odds are lower but agrees the Fed would step in on a serious market dislocation.
insights.speaker: Keith McCullough (host)
insights.so_what: Positions for a long-end bond rally; Hedgeye has flipped from short to long Treasuries (TLT).

insights.claim: Sonders recounts that in February Schwab's internal scenarios did not include Fed hikes this year, and her question about hikes was dismissed — arguing that AI shortens the shelf life of economic drivers, making long-range consensus Fed paths unreliable.
insights.speaker: Liz Ann Sonders (guest, Schwab)
insights.so_what: Don't anchor on consensus rate paths; keep tail scenarios like hikes or abrupt cuts in play.

insights.claim: Schwab clients have shown much more interest in buying Treasuries around 5.2-5.3% on the 10-year, and McCullough names US Treasuries and Chinese stocks as the major asset classes consensus would not buy.
insights.speaker: Liz Ann Sonders (guest, Schwab)
insights.so_what: Long-duration Treasuries at cycle-high yields are a contrarian-but-growing allocation.

insights.claim: Sonders argues investors need 'attribution diversification': holding Mag 7 in equities, the same names' corporate credit in fixed income and AI-heavy private equity/credit leaves portfolios undiversified despite spanning asset classes; long-only hedge funds loaded with mega-cap tech should count as equity exposure.
insights.speaker: Liz Ann Sonders (guest, Schwab)
insights.so_what: Audit look-through exposure to the AI theme across all sleeves.
insights.quote: you might be diversified across asset classes, but you're not diversified from an attribution perspective

insights.claim: Sonders says the cost of servicing US debt exceeding defense spending, $41 trillion in debt and an election driven partly by rage against the billionaire class signal a fiscal and political reckoning, though not a default or loss of dollar reserve status.
insights.speaker: Liz Ann Sonders (guest, Schwab)
insights.so_what: Fiscal concerns are rising into the mainstream; supports term-premium and policy-risk watching rather than default bets.

insights.claim: Sonders warns of a financial-literacy crisis as the line between gambling and investing blurs, citing a 23-year-old who split his family windfall 30% QQQ / 70% SPY believing he 'locked in' positive returns.
insights.speaker: Liz Ann Sonders (guest, Schwab)
insights.so_what: Naive retail concentration in tech-heavy indexes raises wealth-effect and sentiment risk in a drawdown.
insights.quote: I think we have a financial literacy crisis that we're facing given the blurring of the lines between gambling and investing
